paras: The Athens, Georgia, manhunt and lynching threat of February 1888 was a posse's search for an unnamed Black man accused of attempting to assault Miss O'Kelly, the daughter of a justice of the peace, near Athens. Residents declared that he would be lynched once caught, but the last report said he was still at large, and no outcome appears in the coverage.

According to an Athens dispatch dated February 3, Miss O'Kelly was returning to her home, about three miles from Athens, when she met 'a large negro man' who spoke to her in 'very obscene and offensive language' and then attacked her. She broke away and ran home screaming, and the man fled in the opposite direction. Once she told her father, Mr. O'Kelly, a Justice of the Peace, 'a posse of men' set out within minutes to search for him.

He was thought to be hiding near George Murrel's plantation on the Georgia railroad. The dispatch reported that the people of the area were 'thoroughly aroused' and declared 'with one accord that when the negro is caught the verdict of Judge Lynch shall be carried out.' As of 9 o'clock that night the hunt was still going on and he had not been caught.
No report of the man's capture, a lynching, an arrest or a trial was found.

The Savannah Morning News ran the dispatch on February 4 under the headline 'Out of a Fiend's Clutch,' with the subhead 'Narrow Escape of a Young Girl from a horrible Fate.' It treated the accusation as established fact, praised Miss O'Kelly as 'a most lovely young lady' and her father as 'a most worthy gentleman and faithful officer,' and reported the lynching vow without comment. Three days later the Atlanta Constitution printed nearly the same text in a column of Georgia news, closing on the same vow.

The two versions differ on the date: the Savannah dispatch, dated February 3, says the attack became known 'to-day,' while the Constitution says it happened and became known on 'Wednesday,' which was February 1.

accounts.label: Athens dispatch (Savannah Morning News)
accounts.gist: Dated Feb. 3, it places the attempted assault and the alarm 'to-day', describes a posse searching near Murrel's plantation, and reports residents' vow of lynch law; the man was still at large at 9 o'clock.

accounts.label: Georgia news column (Atlanta Constitution)
accounts.gist: The same text with minor changes, dating the attack and its discovery to 'Wednesday' and saying 'Inhabitants of Athens' rather than East Athens; it ends with the lynching vow and reports no outcome.

framing.detail: The Savannah dispatch, headed 'Out of a Fiend's Clutch', presents the accusation as fact, praises the girl and her father, and reports the vow that 'the verdict of Judge Lynch shall be carried out' without objection.
The Constitution reprinted the same account in a state-news column, calling the man 'a negro fiend' and repeating the lynching vow without comment.

conflicts.note: The texts are otherwise nearly identical; the Savannah dispatch is the earlier, dated telegraphic version, while the Constitution's undated column item may have been taken from a weekly source. Neither is clearly better evidence.
Minor wording difference; both put Miss O'Kelly's home about three miles from Athens.
